questions.q: A trader holds a long call option with a delta of 0.60 on a 100-share contract. How would they delta-hedge this position?
options: Sell 60 shares of the underlying short
Buy 60 more shares of the underlying
Do nothing, since delta only matters for puts
Buy another identical call option
questions.explain: Holding -delta shares against the option offsets its exposure. A delta of 0.60 on a 100-share contract is 60 delta-shares of exposure, so selling 60 shares short brings the combined position's delta close to zero.

questions.q: Why does delta-hedging an option require dynamic rather than static hedging?
options: Because options never have a measurable delta
Because static hedges are illegal for options
Because option contracts expire every day
Because delta itself changes as the underlying price moves (gamma), so the hedge ratio must be recalculated and rebalanced
questions.explain: Gamma measures how delta changes as the underlying moves. Because delta shifts, a delta-hedge that was correct yesterday is no longer exactly right today, requiring periodic rebalancing.

options: The risk of a counterparty defaulting on a hedge contract
The risk that a static hedge was never put on at all
The risk that a hedging instrument does not move exactly in lockstep with the exposure it is hedging
The risk that an option's implied volatility is mispriced
questions.explain: Basis risk arises when the hedge instrument and the exposure being hedged don't move in perfect correlation, leaving a residual gap even when the hedge is sized correctly.

questions.q: A jet-fuel buyer hedges fuel costs using crude oil futures because there is no liquid jet-fuel futures market. What is this an example of?
options: A cross-hedge
Delta-hedging
Dynamic hedging
Reverse stress testing
questions.explain: A cross-hedge uses a related but not identical instrument to hedge an exposure when the exact matching instrument doesn't exist or isn't liquid enough — it reduces risk but doesn't eliminate it.

questions.q: When is a static hedge an appropriate choice?
options: Only during periods of high market volatility
Only when hedging options positions
When the exposure being hedged does not change shape over time, such as a linear futures hedge on a fixed exposure
Static hedges are never appropriate in practice
questions.explain: A static hedge is put on once and left in place, which works well when the risk profile of the exposure stays roughly constant rather than shifting as markets move.
